Welcome, everyone! Please note the following security precautions.

 1. First rule: Never disclose or lose your prikey.

 2. Back up your prikey in two or more different locations using two or more methods.

 3. Be extremely careful when generating your prikey using a passphrase. Ensure it is at least 60 characters long and includes at least six random characters. You are facing a global attacker with massive computing power.

 4. The passphrase can generate your prikey at any time, but the passphrase cannot be reversed from the prikey.

 5. When displaying your prikey and passphrase on the screen, ensure your surroundings are secure and out of sight of others, cameras, etc.

 6. If your device is lost or potentially compromised, immediately use your backup prikey to transfer your assets to a secure address.

 7. All on-chain information can be synchronized across any network and device. Please back up any off-chain information yourself.

A Square is an open, on-chain public square.

• No owner or admins. Anyone can join or leave freely, and each join and leave is recorded on the blockchain.

• Its ID is the transaction that created it — there is no central server.

• Any member can edit the name and info, but each edit must burn some Coin-Days (CDD), so spam costs real weight.

• Messages are public and unencrypted — everyone can read them.

Use a Square for open communities. For governed membership or private chats, use a Team instead.

A Team is an owner-managed on-chain organization (protocol FEIP-18).

• It is governed. Unlike a Square, a Team has an owner and managers. The owner can transfer or disband it; managers can invite or remove members.

• Members share a consensus. Joining means agreeing to the team's consensus — its shared rule set — recorded on the blockchain.

• Roles live on chain. Invite, join, leave, appoint, dismiss, rate and disband are all on-chain actions. Its ID is the transaction that created it.

Use a Team for governed groups with managed membership. For open, ungoverned groups, use a Square instead.

An App is an on-chain registry entry for a decentralized application (protocol FEIP-15).

• Anyone can publish. There is no app-store gatekeeper — you register app metadata directly on the blockchain.

• It records metadata. Name, type, home links, download entries, and the protocols, services and code it depends on.

• Its ID (aid) is the transaction that published it.

Apps let people discover and verify decentralized software without a central authority.

Code is an on-chain registry entry for a software artifact — a library, tool or implementation (protocol FEIP-2).

• Anyone can publish. References to software are recorded on-chain without a central authority.

• It records metadata. Name, version, programming languages, homepage links, and the protocols it implements.

• Its ID is the transaction that published it.

Code entries let people find and reference implementations on chain.

A Contact is an encrypted address-book entry stored on-chain (protocol FEIP-12).

• Only you can read it. The chain holds only ciphertext; private fields like names, memos and preferences are encrypted, and only you hold the key.

• It lives on the blockchain. Add, update, delete and recover are on-chain actions, so your contacts are backed up and follow you across devices.

Your contacts stay private to you, even though they are stored on a public chain.

Mail is an encrypted message sent from one FID to another on-chain (protocol FEIP-7).

• End-to-end encrypted. Messages use two-way encryption, so only the sender and recipient can read them.

• Carried on the blockchain. There is no mail server; send, delete and recover are on-chain actions.

• Addressed by FID. No email address or server — just the recipient's FID. You cannot mail yourself.

Use Mail for private, durable messages that depend on no server.

A Token is a fungible on-chain asset (protocol FEIP-20).

• Anyone can deploy one. Deploying fixes its rules — decimal places, optional capacity, and how it may be issued.

• Balances live on chain. Issue, transfer and destroy (burn) move or remove balances; the deployer can close the token.

• Its ID is the deploy transaction.

Tokens are simple on-chain assets whose rules are fixed at deploy time.

A Proof is an on-chain document that records a fact or agreement (protocol FEIP-14).

• Stored on the blockchain. It has a title and body, and its ID is the transaction that issued it.

• Optional co-signing. The issuer can invite cosigners; the proof becomes active once all required signatures are in.

• Transferable. Ownership can be transferred, and the owner can destroy it.

Use a Proof for receipts, certificates, or agreements that need durable, verifiable signatures.

A Protocol is an on-chain registry entry for a formal protocol of the Freeverse ecosystem (protocol FEIP-1).

• Anyone can publish. Protocols are registered on-chain without a central gatekeeper.

• Its ID is the transaction that published it.

Protocol entries let the ecosystem reference and build on shared, openly published standards.

A Secret is an encrypted personal note stored on-chain — a password, key, or any sensitive text (protocol FEIP-17).

• Only you can read it. The chain holds only ciphertext; only the holder of the decryption key can recover the plaintext.

• Backed up on the blockchain. Your secrets persist on chain and follow you across devices.

Secrets keep sensitive information private even though it lives on a public chain.

A Service is an on-chain registry entry for a decentralized service — an API endpoint, storage, relay, or other component (protocol FEIP-5).

• Anyone can publish. Service offerings are registered on-chain without a central authority.

• It records metadata. Endpoints, optional pricing, and links to the protocols and code it uses.

• Its ID (sid) is the transaction that published it.

Services let apps discover and connect to providers across the network.

# Team consensus

## Purpose
What this team exists to do.

## Membership
Who may join, how members are invited, and what is expected of them.

## Decisions
How the team decides things, and who decides what.

## Managers
What managers may do, and how they are appointed or removed.

## Changing this consensus
How this document may be amended. Changing it requires every member to sign the new version, or leave the team.

## Leaving
How a member leaves, and what happens to their obligations.
